utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Very good afternoon to everybody. Could we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian supervised by Ann Sutherland, with Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I didn't know that there was supervision in the OTP. But good to know. For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we immediately continue. I can't identify any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We can. But there is an issue at an appropriate time, Your Honour, that I would like to bring up regarding the documents, the 81 pages that I would request the Court's assistance on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's do it immediately after the break. Then we can restart with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When we finished yesterday, you talked about the blind gentleman who was led by the arm to the restaurant by his friend Becir who was an engineer. You told us what happened --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibrahim Paunovic, his friend. Engineer by profession, Ibrahim Paunovic is the name of the friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what was the fate of Mr. Ibrahim Paunovic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, he, too, was killed in the last days of July, when mass executions of prisoners began to take place in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, were you yourself in the camp ever taken for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about seven days after I was first put into the garage, one of the guards called out my name and took me for an interrogation, to the so-called interrogation room in the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly the nature of the questions you were asked.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I worked in the security service for a long time, and the sort of questions they asked were the run-of-the-mill questions they used to ask everyone. Did I have any weapons? But the most important question for them although they knew me well was what my financial situation was like and how rich I was. That's what they wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you yourself physically mistreated during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unfortunately [as interpreted]. I was lucky not to be maltreated during the interrogation. The interrogators names were Neso Tomcic and Neso Babic, old acquaintances of mine who used to work with me in the Prijedor security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see other prisoners taken for interrogation and return looking different than they had before they went for the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: After my interrogation, my interrogators decided that I shall not return to the garage but instead should be taken back to the pista. According to my own estimate, there must have been between 500 and 700 prisoners already at the pista. And the pista was the best platform to actually see all the things that were happening in the Omarska camp. Every day, except on Saturdays and Sundays, people were called out and taken for interrogation. Many of those would come back bearing obvious marks of torture, beating, and all the other things that had been done to them. Many came back wrapped in blankets. When the guard, who was in the administration building and was in charge of coordination between the interrogators and the guards who were bringing people up there, said: "I need four strong prisoners." And we knew immediately why he was saying that. And then one of our friends, fellow prisoners, who had been taken up for interrogation up there, he was killed during his interrogation. And they needed four physically strong prisoners to take the body out. And they usually dumped the bodies on a lawn, a meadow, to the left of the white house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, may I direct your attention to page 3, line 1. I'm afraid, possibly, there is a mistake, but it should be clarified whether it was really translated into the proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I'm just going to read back the beginning of your answer to one of my previous answers when I asked whether you were physically maltreated. The answer on the transcript reads: "No, unfortunately. I was lucky not to be maltreated during the interrogation." Is that what you meant to say, that you felt it was unfortunately that you were not beaten?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, no. I was not beaten during the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say "unfortunately," do you mean it was -- you were lucky or do you mean that that had some negative consequence?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was lucky. Perhaps I -- yes, I was lucky not to have been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Sivac, something about -- we haven't gone into all the conditions of food and hygiene, et cetera, at the camp. But can you tell us what the physical appearance of the majority of prisoners were? If someone were to come from the outside and look at them, did you and your fellow prisoners appear as you normally would prior to being in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: The prisoners were all in bad shape, and they looked miserable. Having to undergo torture and beating on a daily basis, not having enough to eat and to drink, all this affected the prisoners. And in a short while, they would lose dozens of kilograms. And they would usually get intestinal sickness, and very often it would happen that these prisoners would become incontinent, and all the rooms stank. And many of the older prisoners just couldn't put up physically with all the torture and the beatings and they just died there on the spot. I'll never forget once, in the room, Safet Ramadanovic, a neighbour of mine, died there in the room from all the torture that he had been forced to undergo, and also Meho Habibovic, also died, and all these were elderly prisoners who could not physically tolerate what was happening to them in the camp. And Omer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects himself. Not Omer.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They died due to the results of beatings and difficult conditions in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you now whether you recall any politicians that you recognised visiting the Omarska camp while you were a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: At some point in the second half of July, in the early morning hours, they took all the prisoners out of their rooms and out of the hangar, Burho's room, Mujo's room, from the white house. And they had us lined up usually outside the rooms where they were staying, lined up in several rows. We had our backs turned to the buildings, the rooms, and then Milorad Tadic, Brk, who was some sort of a grey eminence in the camp, was the assistant of Zeljko Meakic, the commander of the camp. But he had a special task to call out the names of the wealthy and distinguished people from Prijedor, take them somewhere, and press them to give him money. And then with a group of guards, he would take them somewhere to collect the money or to find it. And such people who had been called out in such a manner would usually never return to the camp. On that particular day, he was in charge of a ceremony. We did not quite understand what was happening in the camp. From the early morning hours on, we were made to sing their Chetnik songs, as loud and as best we could. And we had to shout their slogans, "this is Serbia, this is Serbia," and they wanted us to lift three fingers. Sometime around noon, from that plateau, we could see a long column, a convoy of vehicles arriving in the camp. At the head of the convoy was the armoured intervention vehicle from Prijedor, and it was followed by another vehicle from which Simo Drljaca and Milorad Vokic emerged. A very comprehensive delegation of politicians came out of the other cars from the convoy. At first, I saw Radislav Brdjanin with a group of collaborators who were in power, and they were the most powerful people in the so-called autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina. There was a group of journalists from Banja Luka, too, people I knew, they were just doing their job. A group of journalists from Prijedor also, and a group of politicians from Prijedor, too, among whom there were Mico Kovacevic, Milomir Stakic, Srdjo Srdic, the inevitable one, was there, too, Simo Miskovic, president of the SDS; Milan Andzic, I'm not sure if I mentioned him. A person from Omarska, he was a very influential man. Radmilo Zeljaja was there, the commander of I think it was the 43rd or 343rd Serbian Brigade which razed Lipik and Pakrac in Slavonija to the ground and then in 1992, Prijedor and Kozarac, and all the rest. During my career, I often attended arrivals of high-state dignitaries, and, for a while, I was in charge of organising Tito's arrivals in Bosnia. Radislav Brdjanin came and was paid the honours and respect that only the top dignitaries ever get. There was the Serbian flag there, and next to it the new Yugoslav flag. Zeljko Meakic saluted in the military way and welcomed those who arrived. And according to military custom, he reported to the president of the autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina, Radislav Brdjanin. For the whole of this time, we had to keep shouting, "this is Serbia, this is Serbia, from Topola to Topola, all the way to Ravna Gora." We were made to sing these songs all the time. And then they started walking. Radislav Brdjanin paused in the middle of the pista and he tried to say something. Amid all the din and shouting, I couldn't hear what he was trying to say. And then they entered the offices above us on the floor where the interrogations were taking place and where the camp administration was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like the witness to be shown, from Exhibit 15, photographs 2, 3, and 18. And if 18 can first be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: While that's being prepared, sir, where were the prisoners at the time that the delegation arrived?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the prisoners had been expelled from the hangar and from the white house and from Burho's and Mujo's room and from the garage, and we were taken to the asphalt plateau outside the rooms in which we were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You talked a bit earlier about the physical appearance of the prisoners. During your stay in Omarska, were prisoners allowed to bathe? Were you given the opportunity to bathe?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Prisoners were not allowed to bathe, and where could they have bathed? Should any of the prisoners have used the lapse of attention on the part of the guards just outside Mujo's and Burho's room, where I spent most of my time, there was a fountain there with running water, but the water was dirty. And for all I know, it was only used for washing the construction machines. And it was not drinking water. And camp inmates could just wash quickly there or drink some of that water, and that was the water we used for drinking. And that's why all of the prisoners had colitis and intestinal diseases and diarrhea and looked miserable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're putting on the ELMO Exhibit 15-18. It will be on your screen. Perhaps you could turn, though, to the photograph on your right, and tell us. We have some other angles of the model we could use if this is not satisfactory. Could you tell us -- can you show us on this photograph where the delegation arrived and where the prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I would first like ask you please to have this photograph. Well, I will try to point it on here. This is going to be a bit unusual. The inmates were outside this room. The garage, the rooms in which Burho and Mujo were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps it might be better if you looked at 15-2. Would this photograph be better for you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I think that -- I think this is the photograph taken from the right angle, the angle I like. So all the prisoners were taken out, outside the hangar. They were lined up here at the pista. And also outside Burho and Mujo's room and the garage. As far as I could see, prisoners were lined up from the white house. When the delegation arrived here at the gate to the Omarska camp, there were two masts flying always a Serbian flag and the flag of the new Yugoslavia. The same flag as before, but without the five-pointed star. So, the main gate to the camp and to the iron ore mines, and then somewhere in this area just in front of us, an APC of the intervention platoon that was escorting the delegation pulled over, and then the car with Simo Drljaca followed by Dusan Jankovic, and they stopped here alongside with Zeljko Meakic, the camp commander. And then in front of Zeljko Meakic, the delegation of politicians led by Brdjanin came out of the car, and then Zeljko Meakic reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could stop you for a moment so we can describe for the record where you were pointing, in describing where the intervention squad and the delegation first arrived, the witness was pointing on photograph 15-2 to the area below the building in the lower right of the photograph. Can you show us where on this diagram you yourself were standing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was here somewhere, just in front of the gate to the room in which I was staying, somewhere in the middle. In front of me, there were several rows. I can't remember how many, perhaps three or four, rows of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness be asked to mark these points on this picture, and then have it as a new exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My supervisor has handed me the copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have another photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Does Your Honour want to call this 15-2B or something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 15-2, it should be a new one, -2I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, why don't you first take the photograph into the desk in front of you, and mark with your initials where you were, and mark with a square where the delegation arrived. I think that is probably too thick to put initials.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The delegation. I'm not sure if this is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The X is where the delegation was. Is that what you're saying? That's the general area?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where Radislav Brdjanin was here, and here behind him were the other politicians. Here, just here on this very spot, Zeljko Meakic reported to Radislav Brdjanin on their way in. And behind Radislav Brdjanin, there were the remaining politicians from Prijedor and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened after they arrived?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We kept singing for the whole time, and yelling "this is Serbia, this is Serbia." And then after Zeljko Meakic reported to Radislav Brdjanin, he walked up to here, I think here somewhere, and then as far as I can remember, for all of them to hear, both the ones and the others, because there was much tumult, and then he said something, part of the delegation going this way passed the prisoners who were here on this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tarmac, and here, there were prisoners here also, those who were staying in the glass house. All the way up to here. They went into the administration building, as far as I knew, and part of the delegation went this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps, you can mark with one of the coloured pens that are just in front of you the line of the prisoners. Why don't you take the red pen, and you've traced a line just so it's clear for the record with a red pen mark how the prisoners were lined up.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were standing here. The prisoners were the garage were here. And the prisoners from Mujo's room were here, and there was a row of prisoners from the glass house here. Here were the prisoners from the hangar and those rooms over there, and here was a group of those who had survived and who were staying in the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Forgive me if I'm incorrect, but I thought when you first talked about the ones in front of the white house, are you sure you saw them or are you indicating some uncertainty about whether the prisoners were outside the white house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sure about that, that there were prisoners outside the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. You mentioned that you saw Mr. Stakic there. How far away from you was Mr. Stakic when he was the closest to you? How close to you did he get during the time you saw him at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure what the distance was, perhaps about 50 metres, between 50 and 70. He was standing to the right. He was in the company of Milan Andzic, as far as I remember. In front of him, Srdjo Srdic and Simo Miskovic headed for the garage. And probably they wanted to take this path to the administration building in order to avoid passing through the rows of prisoners. Perhaps they were afraid that someone would recognise them. And then here, where the prisoners from the garage were standing, the prisoners from this row, Dedo Crnalic walked up to them and asked for something for them to stand somewhere. And then they stood there for a while with Simo Miskovic and Srdjo Srdic. They had a very brief talk, and then they left in a hurry and went behind this garage here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd now like the witness to be given a newspaper article. It is 65 ter number 291. And I hope the booths also have that. If not, I think we have copies. It was distributed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would the Registrar tell me the next S number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would be S238.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So, provisionally 238.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could mark also at this time the 65 ter number -- apparently this was not on the 65 ter list. It was given to the Chambers yesterday and to the Defence on the 11th of July. It is an article entitled -- from Kozarski Vjesnik entitled "Visits, Krajina representatives in Prijedor." Could that be marked 239, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, provisionally 239. And just find out, we got three documents yesterday, no doubt, that I have the correct one in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We do have a couple extras if anyone needs a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before we begin with the article, Mr. Sivac, are you sure you saw Milomir Stakic at the camp that day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in reading yesterday's transcript, I noticed that -- it's my fault -- it was not clear from the transcript who number 5 was in the lineup, the person that Mr. Sivac identified. May the record reflect that was the accused, Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you have been handed a Kozarski Vjesnik article, S238. And I hope the booths have copies. I'd like you to read this slowly, so it can be translated.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read all of it, all the titles and captions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you can start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please, just for your understanding, it's easier for the Judges to have access to these articles in both English and French at the same time. Therefore, we are grateful if you could read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to direct you, sir, I'm only referring to the article entitled: "It's Difficult for Everyone." So if you could read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "It's Difficult for Everyone. 'We fully understand all your problems and admire you for your determination and persistence you have shown in the fight against Muslim and Croatian extremists. But at the same time, we would like you to understand us for not being able to offer you adequate help because of the problems and concerns with which we have to deal.' This was stated during the talks between representatives of the Prijedor and Banja Luka authorities. "For a very long time, almost a month, the Prijedor Municipality was a scene of war clashes and a place kept in isolation of all kinds. For almost two months, the people of Prijedor and their neighbours in Bosanski Novi and Sanski Most fought heavily on a day-to-day basis against Muslim extremists supported by members of the HDZ and HOS. During that time, the Prijedor war unit and the police force lost 43 soldiers, including members of the Serbian Republic of BH, killed in Hambarinsko Polje on the 22nd of May this year when Muslim extremists and members of the Green Berets decided to respond to Alija Izetbegovic's call for a war to the death. The events that followed are more or less known to the public in Prijedor, and even in Banja Luka. Yet, a great deal remains unknown. Yesterday, this should have become obvious to the Krajina representatives, Radislav Brdjanin, president of the AR Krajina War Staff; Radislav Vukic, president of the Banja Luka SDS; Predrag Radic, president of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly; and Stojan Zupljanin, chief of the Banja Luka CSB, for whom some time ago, 500 Muslim extremists led by Hamed Ergelic, Asef Kapetanovic, Elvedin Rizvan, Mirza Mujadzic, and other Prijedor extremists prepared a fiery welcome when the takeover of the Prijedor Public Security Service was to be negotiated. "Having visited the area of war operations and the collection centres, the guests from Krajina thanked their hosts for their hospitality and their ongoing efforts to establish a new Serbian state in this area, especially at this crucial moment when Alija Izetbegovic thinks he has already created a new Alcatraz in Prijedor. "'This is an example of a job well done in Prijedor, and it is a real shame that there are many people in Banja Luka who were still oblivious to this fact, as well as other things that might happen in Banja Luka any moment now. Due to the circumstances in Banja Luka, there is a permanent surplus of Muslims who have fled to Banja Luka from the surrounding municipalities and who have already begun planning how to respond to the jihad. They have been expressing their loyalty only because they are still a minority. As a result of our delusion that they have accepted the Serbian state and the Autonomous Region of Krajina, we have lost 55 men in Kotor Varos, and the Green Berets from Vecici are proud of themselves for killing Stevilovic,' said Radislav Brdjanin. Colonel Vladimir Arsic, commander of the Prijedorska Brigada, Milomir Stakic, president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly; Mico Kovacevic, chairman of the executive committee and Simo Drljaca, head of the Prijedor Public Security Service, acquainted the guests with the general situation and efforts that have been made to normalise living and working conditions, Predrag Radic spoke about the significance of the events in Prijedor and his views concerning Banja Luka. "At present, we all need Banja Luka as a logistics centre. We will continue doing whatever it takes to preserve peace in Banja Luka despite various threats and attempts to cause disturbance. For days now, the Croatian, Austrian, and German media keep accusing Banja Luka of persecution of the Muslims and Croats. Our enemies," -- this is not very clear," -- are resorting to all possible means to malign us, but nevertheless, we are sticking it out. Unfortunately, we have many unresolved problems, one of which is the refugees in the collection centres. The International Red Cross has been trying for days to reach Prijedor, but as we have already stated, we will make it possible for them only after they personally acknowledge the situation of Serbian refugees and captives in Odjak, Rascani, Travnik, Zenica, Sarajevo, Konjic, and in many other places."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could have a seat, because I'm going to ask several questions about this article, before I go on to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, a couple questions about the article you just read. First of all, you were 45 years old in 1992, I believe. You were a former policeman. You were a Muslim. You had left the police because of conflicts with what you felt were Serb nationalists. Were you ever recruited by Mirza Mujadzic or anyone else to take over the Prijedor police station or to engage in any other act of violence?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Mirza Mujadzic despised intellectuals and broad-minded people from the area. He never wanted to have such people around him. For his entourage and for his associates, he chose only people who would listen to him, who would obey him. What I'm trying to say is that he avoided taking professionals, experienced people. He only took members of the Party of Democratic Action. But let me add something to this answer: Whereas at the opposite side, at the Serbian side, this didn't seem to be very important. It was not important for someone to have a membership card, an SDS membership card. They all worked on the same -- with the same agenda. They all espoused the same cause. Their common objective was to ethnically cleanse the Prijedor Municipality and have it inhabited only by Serbs. So for instance, Serbs who were members of the SDP and the reformist forces and all other left-wing parties sided with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In this text, in the last paragraph, it talks about the International Red Cross "has been trying for days to reach Prijedor. But we will make it possible for them only after they personally acknowledge the situation of Serbian refugees and captives in various cities." Prior to the visit of this delegation to the Omarska camp, had the International Red Cross visited the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. They were not allowed access to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In that last paragraph, it talks -- refers to collection centres, and also in the third paragraph, it indicates that the guests from Banja Luka "having visited the area of war operations and the collection centres." What did you understand in the summer of 1992 the word "collection centres" to mean when used by the press of the SDS authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for us, it was ridiculous, the fact that they refer to it as a "collection centre" or "camp" as they called it. It sounded like a summer camp. They obviously wanted to avoid any harsh words that might identify the true character of the Omarska camp. This was all part of the propaganda that even Goebbels wouldn't be ashamed of. Everything that they were trying to do on the territory of the Prijedor area, they were blaming the other side for the same thing. They tried to ascribe this to the members of the opposing party in their propaganda, and we all know that the reality was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can now be shown S239. While that's being prepared, Your Honours, I'm trying to figure out the day of the week the 17th of July would be. I believe the 31st of May would be a Sunday. The 30th of June would be Tuesday, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And indeed, it would be appropriate if we, during this session, could have access to the Kozarski Vjesnik in a way that we can read that it actually was the 17th of July. It can't be identified from the copies before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think we've calculated independently, Ms. Sutherland and I, that the day was a Friday. But we'll double-check and if the Court or anyone has access to a 1992 calendar, we'll double-check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If possible, provide us with the original that we can present also the original to the witness before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We've sent a message asking for that to be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you just to read the short article entitled: "Visits, Krajina representatives in Prijedor." And first, do you recognise from the headline that this is Kozarski Vjesnik from the 17th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, clearly. "Krajina representatives in Prijedor. On Wednesday, representatives from the Autonomous Region of Krajina bodies visited Prijedor, that is, the president of the War Staff Radislav Brdjanin, the president of the regional SDS, Radislav Vukic, the chief of the public security centre, Stojan Zupljanin, and the president of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly, Predrag Radic. During the talks with Crisis Staff members and representatives of the public security station, several topics were discussed. From the functioning of the economy--

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you could slow down.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "to the situation of public security in the area of the municipality. Before these talks, the guests from Banja Luka had made a tour of the municipality where combat actions had taken place and could see for themselves the severity of the clashes with the Muslim paramilitary formations. It has been highlighted in these talks that energetic steps were taken to subdue the activity of the paramilitary formations as in this area, it was realised in time to what an extent -- to what an --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Victims and destruction tolerance of those who had been preparing themselves to settle accounts with the Serbian people for years may lead. In the course of the talks, the representatives of the bodies of the Autonomous Region of Krajina informed the hosts about the steps which the regional government is taking, with the purpose of normalising the situation in this area." To be continued on page 4. I think we've already read that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Sivac, obviously in July of 1992, you were detained. Have you ever seen these articles before this afternoon when you read them?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I see this for the first time. And I have some difficulty, I must admit, reading the Cyrillic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you bring with you to The Hague on this trip a videotape?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And incidentally, so I must be frank, when travelling to The Hague, I was actually coming back from a holiday in Bosnia, I took with me a video which had been sent to me from a colleague in Sweden. But let me try to make this clear: I am preparing a documentary feature currently in Sarajevo -- for the Sarajevo TV. I'm working on this documentary, and many of my colleagues are helping me with the footages that they have. So, one such tape was sent to me by Dzevad Krlebegovic [phoen], a colleague of mine who was now living in Sweden. He remained in Prijedor until 1995, that is, until the time when the ethnic cleansing was finalised in Prijedor, when the last group of Muslims were evicted and expelled through Teslic and Vlasic, and from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, when did you first view the tape that you brought from your friend -- you obtained from your friend in Sweden, and how many times did you look at it, do you think?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received it a year ago, but I have only seen it once. I realise Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the quality was very poor, and that I would not be able to use it for my documentary on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that on the videotape is a short interview with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Initially, I wanted to use this tape for a different footage, that is, I wanted to use a different portion of the tape showing a group of Prijedor residents voluntarily surrendering weapons in the Prijedor barracks because I wanted to show that Muslims and other non-Serbs living in the area of Prijedor Municipality were not in favour of any kind of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Yesterday, when the six persons in the lineup walked into the court, did you have any difficulty in recognising Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. It is a bit of an occupational disease. I'm a professional cameraman, and I need only a fraction of time to remember an image, a face as well. And I can keep it in my mind for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During the lineup procedure, the individuals in the lineup were given instructions to turn at three different angles, but were you looking at them at that time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't really. I didn't pay much interest to the lineup in general because I immediately recognised Dr. Stakic. And I didn't need any more time. I was just waiting for everybody to leave the courtroom so that the identification process can be over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you recognise Dr. Stakic from your dealings with him before the delegation came to the Omarska camp or from seeing him in the media or in person, if that occurred, after that visit of the delegation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, even earlier when he was the vice-president of the municipality, I met him, and that stuck with me, stuck in my memory. But when in 1992 he came over, he looked very different. He was a lot thinner. He didn't wear this beard that he has now. And he was younger, too, like everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The first article that you read today includes information about the Muslims planning a fiery welcome and answering Izetbegovic's call for a war to the death. Was this kind of language typical of the language in the media and used by political leaders at that time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, like I said, Kozarski Vjesnik, the newspaper, and Radio Prijedor were, so to speak, the mouthpiece of the policies implemented at that point by the Crisis Staff. And for a while, articles were not signed, so that the real names of the authors could hide behind the anonymity of those articles. In all of their articles, they actively called on the Serb people to settle their accounts with Muslims and Croats. All Muslims were viewed as Green Berets, and all Croats were viewed as Ustashas. And all the journalists publishing their articles then called on Serb people to finally settle their accounts because the time, they claimed, had come. There was no time to do it during the Second World War, and then during Tito's era, and the time of the communist party it was forbidden, but that now was the time to continue, and enact, in a manner of speaking, the ideology espoused by Draze Mihajlovic and the other Serb leaders, even those from Yugoslavia, I'm here referring to Slobodan Milosevic, as well as in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I'm referring to Karadzic and his collaborators. For all Serb territories to be unified in a single state, to establish the famous territorial axis, Karlovac, Virovitica, and that wherever a single Serb lived had to be Serb soil and Serb state. As an ordinary citizen, I must tell you the following, all these pamphlets were written at the expense and to the detriment of all the other ethnic groups. And I know full well that the Muslim people or the other peoples, non-Serb peoples for that matter, were not in favour of any kind of conflict. Because had they been in favour of clashing, they would have put up some resistance to the police and military coup when there was still a chance of stopping the Serbs from taking over all positions of authority and power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the videotape, it's only about one minute and 5 seconds, I believe, could the videotape now be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I'd ask you to watch the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed in the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "Reporter [on tape]: [Interpretation] Please describe the situation in the territory that is under your control. "Mr. Stakic [on tape]: [Interpretation] Well, I can tell you and the viewers that the whole territory of Prijedor municipality is under our control which I can confirm following the liberation of Kozarac. The town, Serbian settlements, and smaller enclaves with Muslim population have been under our control since the takeover of power on the 30th of April, and now after the fall of Kozarac, the entire municipality is under our control. "In Kozarac itself, the operation of mopping up, as the military call it, is still ongoing because those who are still left there are the most extreme ones and the professionals."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, by the way, could you help us, the body of water that was shown on that video, did you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Water, no, I didn't -- I didn't well notice any water. There must be a creek over there somewhere close to the rail line in the Prijedor area. The rail line passing through Prijedor area and connecting Prijedor with Banja Luka. As far as I could see the location, the Serbs under the bridge there, that was probably in the Trnopolje area or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps if the video could be rewound. It's a minor point. And the translation is not necessary; we can just play that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, on that occasion, did you recognise the water that was in the foreground and some slight hill in the background?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, the quality of the recording is very poor, and I really didn't see any water or anything. I think that must be a field, taken from a wide angle of sorts, so it's not a very clear image. In the background, I can see burning houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you were looking from Trnopolje towards Kozarac, is there a fish farm in between?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, right, there is, there is the Sanicani fish farm. It's a very big one, so it's possible that it was there in the recording. But believe me, I just couldn't identify it because the quality of the image was just so poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in his statement, do you recall if Dr. Stakic, in talking about in Kozarac itself, the operation of, did he use the word in B/C/S "ciscenje"?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he said "we liberated Kozarac." But earlier, he said that they had liberated the remaining areas of Prijedor Municipality, those under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd ask, if Your Honours have the patience, that we just replay the tape. And Mr. Sivac, I'm interested in the last sentence that Dr. Stakic says where he states.. "In Kozarac itself, the operations of..." And then a word, "as the military call it." Can you listen to that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "Mr. Stakic [on tape]: [Interpretation] Well, I can tell you and the viewers that the Prijedor Municipality is under our control which I can confirm following the liberation of Kozarac. The town, Serbian settlements and smaller enclaves with Muslim population have been under our control since the takeover of power on the 30th of April, and now, after the fall of Kozarac, the entire municipality is under our control. In Kozarac itself, the operation of cleaning, as the military call it, is still ongoing because those who are still left there are the most extreme ones and the professionals."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, did you hear the word "ciscenje" in Dr. Stakic's interview?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. The military he said started mopping up the area of Kozarac, and only the most dangerous professionals were left there. And they said that only the most extreme elements were left there, and that the army would soon cleanse the remaining areas of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And yesterday, you described for us the effects of that cleaning that you saw on the ride back from Keraterm to Omarska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're absolutely right. That's the classic term they used, Serb soldiers and Serb officers, well Serb politicians, too. The first time I encountered this expression was when I was covering the war in Croatia. I believed that it would be a fair war, hand-to-hand, but when they started talking about "cleansing" and "mopping up" that was the first time I really saw it for what it was. It was a scorched-earth policy, loot first, then burn, and then demolish. And never again would there be any traces of other civilisations in those areas but the Serb civilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is an appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are still remaining 20 minutes. Could we use this for the documents. You have already Kozarski Vjesnik with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, it has not yet arrived yet. But also the videotape and transcript need to be marked. I forgot to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. The video would be S240. What are the observations by the Defence as regards this video? Do you have any objections? Do you want to see the entire video?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to provisional S240, Your Honour, we would like to view the video in its entirety, but also see if we can obtain from either the OTP or from the video itself, the date of the interview to keep it in perspective, if at all possible, if that's available. With those two provisional, I suppose, objections, we would have no other comments on it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would ask the parties to answer the question now. Do you -- is it necessary to see the entire video? Because it may be necessary to see the entire document, maybe also from that it can be identified the date you just requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Regretfully, Your Honour, we were provided the video in the limited fashion that was submitted to the Court, not in its entirety. So we only have access to that 1-minute and 5-second clip, I believe, although we tried several times yesterday evening to play it we were only able to see this portion that was played here today for the Court this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How long does it take to see the entire video?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I've seen the entire video, but I think it's about an hour. Just to explain, we obtained the video Sunday. It appears to me to have several different recordings on it. I noticed one long section of someone singing, at a wedding or something, it appears to be some kind of social gathering. This video appears to me to be part of a longer news clip, but I did not have the entire news clip translated. I planned to do that, and of course give you a copy of the entire video, and I've asked for the entire tape to be translated, but I put a rush on that one minute of Dr. Stakic's video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The interview started at that moment when we saw the video right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The interview with Dr. Stakic, yes. Before that, there's a -- there is tape showing weapons, as I think Mr. Sivac was referring to, weapons that had been surrendered, from what I gathered from my limited understanding from the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have the video available that we can see the portions immediately before and immediately after?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Certainly. I notice that on the counter, this was at the 37 and a half minute mark, just to give you an idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful to see the portions immediately before and immediately after this clip. But it's difficult now what to admit into evidence. Apparently, you and we have only one minute. There is, we don't know what the remaining is. So we have to leave it open because we can't admit into evidence which might be subject to privacy of the witness before us when it's, indeed, personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe it's not anything recorded by the witness. Mr. Sivac could correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that all of the tape was recorded by your friend? You received the tape as it was? You did not put anything on the tape. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't have recorded this myself. And all the footage on that tape was shot in Prijedor in 1992 by Serb television. So when I received this tape, that was the first time I laid eyes on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also just indicate for the Court that I think I have about another 30 or 40 minutes of direct examination on other subjects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. We leave open the S240. I don't know whether the videodirector is prepared to play in once again, say, two minutes before or two minutes after the clip we saw right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, because they only have the copied tape. We have not yet copied the tape. I'm not even sure if it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's continue with this video after the break. I learned from the registry that the 17th of July, 1992, should be a Friday. This could be checked. And may I ask the usher to present document provisionally 239 to the witness, please. Do you have it before you in B/C/S, Kozarski Vjesnik, 239?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I only have this. I don't have that one. I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please have a look on Kozarski Vjesnik. Is something written over the word "Koz", and what does it read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it reads that this is the war edition. Let me clarify, Your Honour. Exactly at that time in the evening, the ethnic cleansing of the town of Prijedor, Kozarski Vjesnik started being published in this new format. They called it the war edition. And the author of these -- these articles were not signed, probably to conceal their identity. Kozarski Vjesnik very often published public announcements that they would receive from the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality. Announcements on the political and security situation and all the rest in the area of Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence has objections as regards the admittance into evidence of S239A and B, respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour, as those previously outlined, in connection with these articles and publications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you specify in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically with respect to S239, Your Honour, our objection would be there's no author identified in the document. We have not seen the complete set of Kozarski Vjesnik to verify, as the witness has just previously described, the additional stamp that seems to appear on the cover of the article. In addition to that, though limited just to 239, but unfortunately having to compare it to 238, there seems to be some distinction between one certain articles from Kozarski Vjesnik are dated and some that are not. We think it's imperative in order to get all the articles in order to make an assessment, so for both foundational purposes and completeness, we would maintain our objection as we have held to these articles in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Step by step, hopefully we can overcome this when we have the Kozarski Vjesnik edition of 17th July before us immediately after the break. And the same applies for the video. Finally, it has to emphasise to the record that this document, the Page blanche insérée aux fins d’assurer la correspondance entre la pagination anglaise et la pagination française. former S15-2 with additional Roman I with the marks painted on this document, or drawn on this document by the witness, is now S15-2I, and I would ask the registry to provide the parties and the Judges with copies of this document. Then the trial stays adjourned until 4.15. And we start with a short discussion on the 81 documents, and then immediately after this Kozarski Vjesnik and video. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The OTP wanted first of all to address the issue of the 81 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But that has been solved in the meantime, so I don't need to address that now. And in the interests of the time, I want to make absolutely sure we finish with Mr. Sivac so he doesn't have to come back after the break, I'd rather proceed with his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Surprise, surprise. You have withdrawn your objections, or...?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it all depends how you look at it. If the OTP would withdraw their request, then certainly our objection would then be moot. But we just had a very brief conversation about this. I'm not sure if the OTP -- I think they decided this amongst themselves and reached some conclusion that they are going to ultimately share with us with respect to, I believe, the chain of custody issue, but we really haven't in great detail either discussed it, and it was not elaborated to us. So for the record, in all seriousness, we are not withdrawing our objection to those issues, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then I have to ask the OTP to proceed on this issue because time is of the essence, and we have to decide before the Court recess on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the matter that I was going to raise concerned the originals as we've called them, the documents that Mr. O'Donnell seized from the black bag, photocopied, and then turned over to Mr. Inayat who gave them to the OLAD unit. In trying to track down where they went exactly from there, we've discovered since we started this afternoon that actually within one of the documents that we received from Judge Lindholm on the following -- following the seizure, and I believe it has been marked J8, that entire bundle of documents with Dr. Stakic's signature was marked J8 is a document dated the 5th of April which is a receipt from -- signed by Dr. Stakic. It's in B/C/S. It indicates that all items other than, and then it enumerates, I believe, passports, two passports, a driver's license, and one other document, were returned to him. So I don't know -- apparently that document exists already in the Court exhibits as part of J8. There's another receipt which we haven't yet produced in court, but it indicates that car keys and insurance paper and one document which has a title of I'm going to try to pronounce it, but -- I'll spell it -- car documents, And then in front it's indicated "S-A-O-B-R-A-C-A-J-N-A Prometna Dozvola," two other words, an international motor insurance card, a set of house keys, and a set of car keys. We have given to Mr. Lukic to pass on to those who could, in his -- in Dr. Stakic's family who needed those items. And just as I stated before, that particular document -- There is one document in those 81 pages that's labelled "Saobracajna prometna dozvola" is not one of the eight pages that has the disputed signatures. But just to complete the picture of where all those 81 pages went to, at least one of those documents, it's several of the 81 pages because I think there were four pages of those documents copied were given to Mr. Lukic, apparently to give to the defendant's family, I presume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any observation to this? Is Defence contesting the report of Judge Per Lindholm?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Certainly, not, Your Honour. We would not at this time do that. And we don't anticipate, in any way, taking any exception with the report by the Court or Your Honour who submitted that report. However, I want just want the record to be clear that our objections do not merely just go to the issue that the OTP is now on today's date raised in essence, they have still failed to address the critical issues that we thought we raised in our objection, namely, the illegal search and confiscation of the personal effects of Dr. Stakic, although we can debate, and I don't have it before me, the issue of Dr. Stakic signing a simple form which says all items were returned to him. However, once we commence that debate, it only highlights our prior commentary which clearly we felt, based on the testimony by Mr. Bernard O'Donnell, were the policy in every criminal and investigatory jurisdiction requires there to be a specific detailed inventory. Simply put, it's that inventory prior to this return of documents as the OTP has asserted that only makes it more critical and crucial, I think, which would in our opinion have our objection sustained on those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But these observations we heard already yesterday, and we exchanged the opinion. And I think there is now nothing new on the issue of the alleged illegal seizure. So it's only where are the documents, and this is -- seems to be a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps to complete the picture, this receipt signed by Mr. Lukic which the Defence was honourable enough to submit to us should be marked as an exhibit also. It was a filing, so I believe the Court has it. I believe it was also filed with the Court. In any event, you can mark this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Until now, I haven't seen it, but this is another question. So it should... It's up for the parties to decide, S or D?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have no objection to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it should be S241. And admitted into evidence as S241. And indeed, apparently one picture of what happened later to the documents. The other issue, no doubt, remains. Then what about Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have the original, and Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the usher please present it first to the Defence and then to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And the articles in question are on page 1 and page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think in the meantime, the usher can bring in the witness, to save time. In the meantime also, in order to save time, may the video director please play once again, as requested, the video. And additional two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "Reporter [on tape]: [Interpretation] We're talking now with Milomir Stakic, the president of the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff. Mr. Stakic, describe to us please the situation in the territory that is under your control. "Milomir Stakic: I can tell you and the viewers now that the whole territory of Prijedor Municipality is under our control following the liberation of -- which I can confirm following the liberation of Kozarac. The town, Serb settlements, and smaller enclaves with Muslim population have been under our control ever since the takeover of power on the 30th of April. And now, after the fall of Kozarac, the entire municipality is under our control. In Kozarac itself, the operation of cleaning, as the military call it, is still ongoing because those who have stayed behind are the most extreme ones and the professionals."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, it may be stopped for now. Maybe it's necessary to come back to the one or other clip in this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that be rewound about one minute to the point where there's a house that's shown and I believe it has a blue flag on the corner. I couldn't tell what that was. I was going to ask the witness if he could recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For clarification, I think we had already a discussion on this. If the interpretation could be quite clear whether the word used has to be translated as "cleaning" or "cleansing" because now it reads on the transcript "cleaning." It was, of course --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one could translate it with cleaning, cleansing, or mopping up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, we could go forward from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, there's a house in the photo coming up. I'm going to ask that the picture be stopped. And I just saw something hanging and I want to see. If we could stop the picture now. Do you see on the upper left of the screen, there's a -- something hanging from the roof, it appears to be blue and white?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, it's a white flag or a white sheet that the person living in this house must have hung out as a sign of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can the witness please explain the -- in the clip just before the interview with Dr. Stakic, which area has been shown there when we saw fire, places.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, the footage that we saw a moment ago is a recording devised by one of the most extreme journalists, Rade Mutic. He himself read out the text, he makes mention of jihad warriors in his comment and foreign mercenaries, something which we did not see in this footage. All we were able to see was a large number of Muslim villages, such as Jakupovici, Kamicani, and other areas inhabited of -- by Muslims in the greater area of Kozarac, and a large number of Serb military and police officers supervising the area. They were probably waiting for all the property to burn down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's necessary. We can't continue with the video only in portions, in small portions. Therefore, I believe it's necessary that the OTP is prepared to have an in-depth look into the entire video and to present those portions they regard as necessary for their case tomorrow in the presence of the witness because without additional comments given by the witness before us, it may have less probative value and something is not self-explanatory for us. Therefore, I would ask the OTP to proceed this way, as indicated, and only then we have a reasonable basis and now know what we really admit into evidence. So today, a decision on S240 is not yet ripe. We have to come back to this video for evident reasons. What about Kozarski Vjesnik? May the usher please bring the newspaper to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the OTP, the document immediately over the article read out today, did we already admit this article into evidence? Because in the context of what the witness has told us immediately before the break, the article immediately above would enlighten the context of what the witness has told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Is Your Honour referring to page 1 or page 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Page 1. If the usher could please present this article to the witness, and may I kindly ask the witness once again to read this additional article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please, slowly, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Regional staffs appointed. The Crisis Staff has appointed members of the regional staffs in ten areas." This is illegible. "Of territorial units of the Prijedor Municipality," I guess. "Due to the war, the regional -- as a result of war events, the regional staffs should be vested with authority in the upcoming period of time with the main task being taking care of the security issues on the territory they are in charge of. The president of the regional staff Ljubija is Slobodan Taranjac, and his deputy is Milenko Jelisavac. The president of the regional staff Prijedor I is Srdjo Srdic with Mr. Djordje Kostic as his deputy. Mr. Marinko Colic has been appointed president of the regional staff Prijedor 2, and Dusko Vejnovic as his deputy. As for the regional staff of Lamovita, Mr. Vinko Kos has been appointed president, and Mr. Borislav Grahovac as his deputy. Whereas the president of the Omarska regional staff will be Mr. Bozo Mandic with Mr. Sveto Kremenovic as his deputy. Tukovi regional staff, president Slavko Antonic, with Mr. Radovan Cetic as his deputy. "Orlovaca regional staff, Mr. Ranko Nikic has been appointed president, and Mr. Radanko Goronjic his deputy. Mr. Milorad Raus has been appointed president of the regional staff, Brezicani, and Mr. Milan Babic has been appointed as his deputy. Mr. Zdravko Jovic has been appointed president of the regional staff, Rakelici and Mr. Dusan Kurnoga has been appointed his deputy. The Crisis Staff is of the opinion that the work concerning the establishment of these staffs has been delayed which has an impact on certain actions of the new government in the Prijedor Municipality. That's why the Crisis Staff is going to insist for certain measures to be undertaken as soon as possible, so that the organs of the government can start functioning in a satisfactory manner. "The above-mentioned staffs will soon receive a decision containing sanctions in cases -- the relevant decisions of the new authorities are not adequately and timely carried out." [As read]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Now, in the order, 238, objections by the Defence? 238.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, previously we raised two specific items as a bases for our objection. One, namely, the date of the article, since on page 4 it's rather clear from reviewing the original, on the left-hand side, one can ascertain the date that's cited. So we would withdraw our objection to that. However, we must maintain our objection and continue to object, with respect to the article that the OTP is suggesting be introduced into as evidence, as to its authorship. Interestingly enough, though, when we've had our first opportunity to review an original document from Kozarski Vjesnik, we note that within page 2 at the bottom, there is an editorial staff mentioned as well as, perhaps, from other articles, we would be able to glean the bases or the premises upon which some of these articles are written, which we think would then maybe overcome our objection as to relevancy, foundation, and authenticity. However, until we review all those original documents in their complete form, we must maintain our objection on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, Document S238A and B respectively admitted into evidence. The same is true for 239?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, S239A and B respectively. And to continue, because this seems to be a very special edition of this, of Kozarski Vjesnik, I should like to ask the OTP to provide us with colour copies of pages 1 to 4 of this edition of Kozarski Vjesnik. And if I understand correctly, these documents are tendered by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then these four pages could be S241, page 1 is -1, page 2, -2; page 3, -3; page 4 -4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe you had previously indicated that S241 would be the receipt signed by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you. Then 242. Sorry for my mistake. Then we have only to come back to the video tomorrow, and now, please, proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, on the interview tape of Mr. Stakic, did you recognise the journalist who was interviewing him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. His name is Predrag Laketa. He worked for the Serb television in Banja Luka, and I think he still works for the Banja Luka TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back now to some of the events in the Omarska camp. You had mentioned at one time your sister being taken to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the camp. Did you see her in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw her very often. My sister was in a group of 36 women who would often sit in one of the corners of the restaurant when we went there to have our meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you have any information about how the women in the Omarska camp were treated?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do, although, although all of the women who were with us in the Omarska camp, including my sister, are reluctant to talk about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you or the other prisoners ever hear anything coming from the rooms where the women were at night?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was at night next to Buhro's and Mujo's room, that is, above our two rooms, there are offices where interrogations were carried out and where women were kept at night. Horrible things happened at night. Almost throughout the night we were able to hear furniture breaking accompanied by the screams and moans of women. They were crying for help. And at night, when the camp became quiet, upstairs, above our heads, things would be going on that were beyond our comprehension. I mean, we could only assume what was happening to those women upstairs. During the day, when we went for lunch, which was the only meal that we had, we saw these women in the restaurant. They were distributing food there. And we could tell, that is, we would observe on their faces marks and traces of abuse, torture, and beatings. There was a large number of women who had bruises on their faces, bruises that were the result of torture and assaults. Their faces and their arms were black and blue. So it was perfectly clear to us what was going on during the night in those offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You told us earlier that your sister was a judge. Did you see any other judges in the camp detained as inmates?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many people in the Omarska camp who had previously worked for the judiciary. Nedzad Seric, the president of the Prijedor court, was in my room, for instance. Eso Mehmedagic was there as well. He worked for the attorney's office in Prijedor. Omer Kerenovic was there, as well, a judge. Ahmet Atarovic, a defence lawyer from Prijedor was also there. Defence attorney Trozic [phoen] from Prijedor, Silvije Saric, a lawyer from the PTT. There were quite a few of them. Ismail Burazovic also, who worked as a lawyer in the public construction and utility company. There were many people who were lawyers by occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned Judge Omer Kerenovic. Did Judge Kerenovic have any physical disability?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was disabled. He had an invalid arm, the right arm, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was the fate of Judge Kerenovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the individuals that I have mentioned were killed in Omarska, in 1992. A long time ago now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that you yourself were not beaten during the interrogation. Do you recall one day, a particular bad day, when you were taken or going to the restaurant and you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody was beaten in the camp on that day. The shift which was on duty, and which was led by Mlado Radic, Krkan, organised or set up a gauntlet of guards when we went to the restaurant to have our lunch there. They were assisted by the guards from other shifts. And on that day, almost the entire day, from the early morning hours until late in the afternoon, they beat the detainees in a most brutal fashion. Of course, I had to go to lunch in one of the groups, and I was among the first members of the group who entered the restaurant. The actual entering to the restaurant was very harsh. We received a lot of blows, but we somehow managed to get in. The guards had thrown various objects on the floor, pieces of furniture, pieces of glassware, shattered glass, and they poured oil on to the floor so that the surface would become slippery. But -- and when we finally got in the restaurant, we didn't care much about food. All we could think of was how to get out in the safest way possible. Mlado Radic was standing there and at one point he motioned to us to start moving towards this row of guards, being large and stocky, I stood at the head of the column. I was trying to protect others who were running behind me. Marjan Zec who used to work at the local bank in Prijedor was behind me. And as we were passing by the pista, we could see people screaming, falling down all over the place. I remember that on that occasion, the guards had special objects, specially designed for beating for that occasion. They had baseball bats, pieces of metal chains with balls attached to them. And when I thought that that was the end of it, that I had managed to get through, I received a terrible blow in my head. All of a sudden, everything became dark. And after a while, I don't know how much time elapsed, maybe 20 minutes or half an hour, I came to, and I heard voices of the people I knew. I had been carried out on to the pista. And Mustafa Muhic was actually holding me. Said Baric his colleague was next to him. And there was Dr. Esad Sadikovic standing above me trying to help me and he was wiping my head with some cloth. I heard that -- I remember that a guard --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the name of the guard.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Hit me with this piece of metal chain that had a metal ball attached to it on my head. And I have a scar that I know I will bear as a souvenir for as long as I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall a young man by the name of Smail Duratovic being brought into your room one day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Smail Duratovic, he was a well-known athlete from Prijedor. He played football. He stayed with his father in Buhro's and Mujo's room, in our room. One day, it was Petrovdan, St. Peter's Day, it's a very important saint for the Serbs, guards came for him, took him away, out of the room, and he was sitting with them outside. We saw them as we were going to the restaurant to get our meals. And also on the way back to our room. In the evening hours, they took him towards the white house, and somewhere on the tarmac outside the white house, they set fire to a tyre, a rubber tyre. And Smail Duratovic was thrown into that burning tyre. Again, I must emphasise that it was a holiday for the Serbs and the guards were drunk, heavily. They sang and shouted and somehow they behaved in a special way on that day. But in the evening hours, fortunately for Duratovic, it began to rain. He took advantage of the absence of the guards who left and headed for the place where food was distributed. There was some sort of a room there in which they kept liquor. So he managed to sneak in the direction of the white house and to get in there somehow. The day after, the camp inmates who came from the white house through their wives, he sent word to his father that he was alive and that he was in the white house. And his father tried to organise for him to be transferred to Buhro's and Mujo's room, otherwise he would be killed the same night. And through Buhro's and Mujo's assistance, and Dr. Esad Sadikovic's assistance, too, his father managed with the help of a guard whose last name I think was Krivaja to bring Smail Duratovic over. And he looked horrible. Most of his clothes had been burned. He was all black, as though he had fallen through a chimney. On his arms and legs, you could see burns. He couldn't speak. He just babbled. We all assembled there in that room, and then Dr. Eso chased us away, told us to go away. And then he tried to help him, applying some pomade, some cream from the women -- he had obtained from the women in the camp. And then there was a litre of brandy that the lawyer Ahmet Atarovic had obtained through a guard. So using this brandy, he tried to treat his wounds, so Duratovic made it. He survived the Omarska camp, and he was taken to Manjaca with a group of sick people and people who needed medical assistance, and then with the assistance of the Red Cross, he was transferred somewhere abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You talked about the types of people, the types of occupational groups, that were targeted in the camp. Were those who were wealthy and those that were successful entrepreneurs targeted?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no rules really. It all depended on what the guards' mood was and what their orders were, who was to be executed, who was to be abused and tortured and so on. Mainly, however, they didn't really care whether anyone was a member of the SDA or the HDZ or any of the nationalist parties. They treated us all the same mostly. They would tell us: "You'll all be executed. We will execute the lot of you." They told us openly. And as my sister told me later, she had known Zeljko Meakic, the camp commander, from her experiences as a judge. And she told him: "Zeljko, please, if my brother Nusret is on your list, please rather kill me, because I'm alone, I have no family. And my brother has two children."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
