utterances.text: Do you recall a businessman by the name of Zlatan Besirevic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatan Besirevic, an engineer, he was one of the best businessmen in Prijedor, entrepreneur. He was very young when he set up this factory which was very successful and they were exporting their products abroad. He was in the room together with us in Buhro's and Mujo's room, and please, Your Honours, let me point this out to you, his father Kemo was a Muslim, and his mother, Draginja, a Serb woman. But he too, was brought to the camp. And then through some family connection his mother had, he managed to have his name added to a list of elderly and sick people who were supposed to be transferred to the Trnopolje camp. So he managed somehow to have his name included on that list. The names of those people were called out, and then these people were separated from the rest and left in a corner of the pista to wait for a bus to take them away. We all envied them because leaving for Trnopolje meant salvation for all of us who were in Omarska. However, they stayed at the pista for several days. And apparently, the guards who organised the transfer told them that the bus could not make it to the camp because they had no fuel. When eventually, after four or five days, the bus arrived to take away the people who were meant to be transferred to Trnopolje, Zeljko Meakic personally read out the list. And once he had called out all the names, he just added: "Zlatan Besirevic must stay in the Omarska camp until further notice." We were all taken aback. We were listening to this. We were at the pista because we had just come back from our meal. And engineer Zlatan Besirevic was the most surprised of us all. He stayed back and talked to Zeljko Meakic about something, and the lot of us, he went back to Buhro's and Mujo's room, and after a while, he returned too. And he was desperate. When we asked him why he wasn't being transferred to Trnopolje, he said: "My name was taken off the list, removed from the list, in the Crisis Staff." A day later, late in the afternoon, which was quite unusual, they -- around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, they came to take away Zlatan Besirevic, and the guards were really brutal. He had to put his hands behind his head and run, and he was led towards the red house whence he never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned at the end of the day yesterday the names -- you began to name doctors who had been at the camp and had not survived.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the greatest tragedy for Prijedor, for my town, for my municipality, is that in that tragic year of 1992, a doctor, a medical man, was at the head of the municipality who had taken the oath of Hippocrates, and he was supposed to be some sort of a humanist. But in an indirect way, by whose orders I don't know, most of the doctors who were at the Omarska camp, Muslims or Croats, were killed. Their only fault is that they had a different last name and they belonged to the wrong ethnic group. Out of respect and piety, I will mention their names, Dr. Jusuf Pasic, Dr. Osman Mahmuljin. I will not list their professional credentials now. Dr. Zeljko Sikora, Dr. Enes Begic, Dr. Rufat Suljanovic, and I'll mention Islam Bahonjic also. He was a person who was an x-ray technician at the Prijedor hospital. He had worked there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You've mentioned a couple times in your testimony Dr. Esad Sadikovic, who treated you and treated Mr. Smail Duratovic. Do you recall the last time you saw Dr. Sadikovic? First, can you tell us what kind of person was Dr. Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To talk about Prijedor, the town, to talk about these camps, the tragedy, and to omit the name of Dr. Eso Sadikovic would be a sin. He was a deeply humane person. And he helped everyone, whatever their religious background or colour of skin. He was a UNHCR expert, and he had spent a long time working somewhere in the Pacific, in Libya, in a number of African countries helping people. He was a charismatic person in the town of Prijedor. He knew it, and he was proud of it. In the Omarska camp, he did his best to help whoever he could. And where no one was willing to go and to help, he was always there to do it. He was even helping Serb guards there, who come to take up their shift. They were dead drunk and times they were wounded and they had skirmishes among themselves, and they quarrelled over money and how to distribute the money they had looted. And he helped them, too. And after most of the Prijedor doctors, or at least those who were in the camp had been killed, the authorities in Prijedor knew very well that a finishing touch was to be added. I'll never forget that night, because that was the last night in the Omarska camp. It seemed a quiet night at first, but just before dawn broke, a guard appeared at the door, and he said: "Dr. Eso Sadikovic, come out and take your stuff with you." We were surprised because we knew that his name had been called out very often, but this time they told him to bring his stuff. So we knew where they were taking him. Dr. Eso stood up. He took his nylon bag in which he had a handful of cigarettes that the other prisoners had collected for him. He brought his dirty shirt, and he headed for the door. We all stood up. We stood quietly. And then all of us started -- all of us spoke out loud, and he said -- and we said: "Dr. Eso, thank you, thank you so much for everything." He just turned back and he said: "Thank you, friends. And goodbye." We did not believe that there was such a criminal person in this world who would be able to kill a man like Dr. Eso.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was the date that you left the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left on the 7th of August. I was in a group that was transferred to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are we going to 5.30, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you so want, until 5.50.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Trnopolje camp -- I'm not going to ask you in detail about that camp, but can you tell me, first of all, in the camp were you free to leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we should take a break now, Your Honour, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 5.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, when you arrived in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, after you arrived in the Trnopolje camp on the 7th of August, were you free in that camp to leave at any time you wanted?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in the Trnopolje camp, it was surrounded with wire fencing. It was fenced off with wire, and there were guards standing by the fence. But as opposed to the guards at the Omarska camp, these guards we knew because they were people from Prijedor. My long-time collaborator, newspaper journalist, Boro Grubic was manning one of the command posts. Ten years ago, we worked together. I was the cameraman and he was the journalist. The third member of our team, Burho Kapetanovic, who was an audio technician, he was no longer around because Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he had been killed in Omarska on the 27th of July, 1992. The people we found upon our arrival in the Trnopolje camp were also acquaintances from Prijedor, from Kozarac, people we knew. The day before, people from the Keraterm camp had been brought to the Trnopolje camp. And yes, the conditions in the Trnopolje camp were much better than those in the Omarska camp. But those who had been there in the Trnopolje camp for a longer time advised us to really watch out for ourselves because even in this camp, they did still kill people. One of the groups that had arrived in Trnopolje before our own transfer, a group that had been there before we arrived, Anto Murega and his son Zoran, as well as Laus, Remet [phoen], a well-known butcher from Prijedor, were singled out, taken off, and then killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end of August, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: While you were at the camp, did you hear from others who were detained there anything regarding sexual assaults of women who were in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when we came there, we found people, mostly from the Kozarac area, who had been brought to Trnopolje on the 25th, 26th, 27th, and 28th of May, when the ethnic cleansing of Kozarac began. And they told us that even here, dreadful things were happening. Very often, when returning from the front line, Serb soldiers and among them soldiers who had been manning tanks, would arrive just outside the camp, and then pick for themselves women and girls, take them away at night, and then return some of them in the morning, but some were never returned to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In order to be released from the camp, what did you do? Whose signature -- whose approval did you have to get?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to leave Trnopolje, there were several conditions to be met. One of the main conditions was to give money or other valuables. Release papers, the release papers from the Trnopolje camp were signed by Slobodan Kuruzovic, the commander of the camp, and Pero Curguz, who was there on behalf of the Serbian Red Cross. Let me also mention this, Your Honours: Despite all, after several days of our stay in Trnopolje, we were ordered to remove all the wire from the fencing around the camp. And then Serb guards brought a big board with a writing on it "collection centre." This was all happening around the 10th of August, 1992. We did not exactly understand why this was happening. But in the afternoon hours, Zeljko Meakic, the camp commander of Omarska, brought several TV crews, there, foreigners. And among them was a TV crew from Pale, my erstwhile friends who used to work for Sarajevo television. They brought them there to show: "Look, here you are. There are no more camps in the Prijedor area. These are only collection centres." That people were not fenced off from the rest of the world in these collection centres and that the treatment we were being given was almost humane.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you get a permission slip, a release slip, signed by Kuruzovic and Curguz and released from the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the last days of August, at the Trnopolje camp, or collection centre as it came to be called, a TV crew from Prijedor arrived. Rade Mutic, who was the author of one of the reports that we have seen, and Zivko Ecimovic, his collaborator, they were putting together some programme on the Trnopolje camp. And then they looked at me, and they said: "Well, Omarska could not be helped." The release papers for someone to leave Omarska would have had to be signed by someone from the Crisis Staff directly, or by Radmilo Zeljaja, the commander of the 43rd Motorised Brigade. And then they asked me whether I was willing to leave Trnopolje and to go home. And as anyone else would have said, I said: "Of course, yes. I would like to leave." I didn't know where my family was. And they went to some offices there, the administrative offices in Trnopolje, and there they drew up a paper, some sort of release papers for me, which I used to leave the camp and go back to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you go back to the apartment you had been living in before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not supposed to because my wife and my family had fled to stay with our friends in the Puharska settlement. And there was a sign on my door saying "occupied by a Serb soldier" apparently, and I'm not sure what unit that particular soldier belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you stay in Prijedor until December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During the time you were in Prijedor, you talked earlier about before your arrest some of the parts of the town being targeted or destroyed. Did you see neighbourhoods of Prijedor that had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was there for all to see. And without those areas which had been destroyed, Prijedor, the town, looked mutilated. Stari Grad, the old town, was wiped off the face of the earth completely. Parts of the Partizanska Street, almost the whole Muharem Suljanovic Street, and all the houses in that street close to the Bereg creek, and all mosques and all monuments to Islam had been destroyed, as well as the Catholic church in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: These areas that you talked about like the streets that you named, Partizanska Street and others, did they tend to be areas populated by a particular ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those areas were mostly inhabited by Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned before that you had spoken once to an architect, I believe, who had taken part in some of the demolitions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was released from the camp, and during my stay in Prijedor, I saw a committee led by Dule Miljus, civil engineer from the Ljubija iron ore mines, Veljko Hrgar, an architect, and some other people I didn't know, they were visiting the areas that were mostly populated by Muslims and Croats. And they marked off those houses which were still in good shape, houses that had not been torn down. And then at night, you would hear powerful explosions. They used explosives to demolish these houses, and then the next day, cranes and construction vehicles were brought over to collect the rubble and take it somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In your conversations with -- did you speak to one of these two individuals, either Dule, the civil engineer, or the architect regarding who had ordered this action?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the people on that team went abroad after a while. And I met him there. He was married to a Muslim woman. And after I published my articles in the Oslobodjenje newspapers, in which I described the events in Prijedor, he apologized to me, he told me "we had to do it, and the orders were given by the Crisis Staff. Certain parts of the town and the Muslim quarters, which did not exactly fit our new urban planning scheme, simply had to be torn down."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that Exhibit 294 be shown to the witness. 65 ter number 294. It does not yet have an S number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so. That be provisional S243.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to summarise the document for the record, is it correct, Mr. Sivac, that the document in front of you indicates that it's a decision of the executive committee from a meeting on the 21st of July, adopted the following decision on the demolition of structures damaged beyond repair in the course of combat activities. It then lists addresses of many structures. Many of these I see on the first and second page of the English translation, it's on the first page, I believe, on the B/C/S copy, are a street called Babica Street. Do you recognise the street name?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Generally speaking, this entire list, I mean, all of these buildings were located in the old part of town such as Ahmet Babic Street and so on and so forth. All of these locations were in the old town in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. In order -- in order to leave Prijedor, did you ever have to sign any documents or obtain any documents from the municipal authorities, and if so, what were those documents?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's my wife who dealt with these things, mostly. I tried to avoid public appearances of all sorts. I had to obtain a number of certificates and take care of the paperwork. There were things that we had to pay if we wanted to leave the area. There was also the transit visa that we had to obtain. Then the Red Cross would transfer these people to Novska, and then from there, wherever people managed to go to. Sometime in November 1992, I had another unpleasant experience. I was again arrested. My detention was ordered by Milutin Cado, a deputy to Simo Drljaca. The reason for it was a banal one. Allegedly, it was about my apartment. But he was interested in other things as well. He inquired about my sister, for instance, who had managed to flee to Croatia, thanks to some connections that she had at the time. And one of the things that he wanted to charge me with was the allegation that I had recorded the destruction of the Catholic church and the mosque in the area, and that I had sent this footage to foreign companies, foreign TV companies. And I said to him: "Well, you arrested me months ago. And you forced me to turn over all the technical equipment that I had. So you know that I didn't have adequate equipment to do it." And he said: "Don't play with me. I know that there are things -- that there were still things that are hidden." Then he took me to the police station in Prijedor, and he ordered that the Sivac family should remain in Prijedor until further notice, despite the fact that we had already collected all of the necessary papers. I realised that I was again being targeted, not only myself but my family as well. And it was clear to me that he would kill me. If not him, then one of the groups led by Zoran Zigic or other local thugs who were supposed to take care of the remaining Muslims in Prijedor. But I managed to organise my secret departure from Prijedor through a private agency in Gradiska. The chief of this agency was Jankovic, a local lawyer, and his wife Ljiljana. We managed to collect the little property that we had or the things that we could take with us, and I finally managed to leave for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When did you leave for Croatia? Was that in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the 17th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Prior to leaving, did you have to renounce any property that you had in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had to renounce all the property that I had in favour of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I want to thank you. I have one final question. You had testified previously, am I correct, and you've indicated a willingness to come and testify in other trials. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider it to be my moral obligation and my obligation as a human being to assist this Tribunal in trying all of those who are suspected of having committed crimes in my homeland, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, regardless of their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's appropriate and fair to ask the following two questions before we start the cross-examination, allowing by doing so the Defence to include the answers in the cross-examination already. My first question is the following: Did you -- do you know something about the question whether or not Dr. Stakic retired from his office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. While I was still in Prijedor, that is, before my departure, I think he was still in office. I don't know what happened later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would mean -- you said you left to Croatia mid-December, 17th of December, 1992. In your opinion, Dr. Stakic was still in office at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly, I don't know. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. That's quite clear when you don't know, please say so. The second question: No doubt you are aware of the importance of your testimony. And as you correctly stated just before, you wanted to assist us, the Judges, this Tribunal, to come as close as possible to the truth to find justice. Justice can't be found on the basis of possible unfounded judgements. The basis for our judgement can only be documents and the statements of witnesses. One part of your testimony of today might have a crucial impact on the outcome of this case. And therefore, please don't misunderstand when I recall that you give your testimony under solemn declaration. And therefore, I want to ask you once more: Are you quite sure, is there no doubt for you, that you in fact saw Dr. Stakic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have it before your eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I still do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's appropriate to give some time in preparation for the Defence. And we start the cross-examination tomorrow only, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be acceptable, Your Honour, but I'm not sure if the Court would like to address the admission of S243. We do have a preliminary observation and comment on that. However, if the Court could indulge me, I would prefer to argue that or share with the Court our bases without the presence of the witness being here, if we're going to break and commence tomorrow, it might be more appropriate and polite to do so outside of his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the witness has had a difficult day. And we understand how difficult it must be for the witness to give this statement. And therefore, I would ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before the witness leaves, can I just ask, does the Defence believe that we can complete the cross-examination tomorrow? Because I just want to remind everyone that otherwise it would not be until after the break, the witness would have to come back after the summer break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The maximum would be 50 minutes in addition on Thursday in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In part, yes, Your Honour. Quite frankly it was my understanding that we would proceed on Thursday from 10.15 until approximately 2.15 which would, based on the schedule provided by the Court, we would have an additional hour and a half following the videolink. It's my understanding that the witness through the videolink is confined to that timeframe. And that was shared with us, I believe, yesterday. So we would have additional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What I learned was 10 to 12.15. But Madam Registrar possibly can correct me. Please, give it to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just received an updated calendar. However, the system isn't allowing me to open the document. So if you can just give me a few minutes, but that is what I was informed yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We come back to this, but first I think it's appropriate that we excuse the witness for today. And we thank you for your testimony of today. And the usher, please, escort now the witness out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then, before we get the information from the registry, the admission into evidence, S243. Your objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly, the observation that I would like to make in connection with this exhibit 243A and B is as follows: First of all, obviously we're going to continue to maintain our objection on authenticity and signature which has not been established by the OTP. Secondly, and quite frankly, critically, the OTP started and elicited testimony from the witness there were orders given by members of the Crisis Staff on or about the events that transpired and purportedly are reflected within this Exhibit S243A and B. Nowhere within that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. exhibit does it mention the Crisis Staff. I think that it is -- if it's an attempt to impeach the witness and to suggest to the witness, since he testified on page 53, lines 23 through 25, and then proceeding also on page 54, lines 1 through 3, that it was the orders of the Crisis Staff, we would not object to this document being presented. If it was an attempt to try to refresh the witness's recollection as to who may have given the orders, not the Crisis Staff as the witness initially testified to, then again, we would not have an objection to the document. To allow the document, based on the testimony by the witness, we believe will cause undue confusion and will not, given the Defence's standpoint, will not bring any clarity to the issues that are necessary for resolution before the Chamber. For those reasons, Your Honour, since -- although I won't speculate, do not believe the intent was to impeach the witness or to refresh his recollection, since there were no follow-up questions, we would object to the submission at this time of S1243A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Comments in response, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I think our position throughout has been clear, that the executive committee is a subordinate body, subordinate in normal times to the Municipal Assembly and the president of the Municipal Assembly. That has been the evidence from the witnesses. And the evidence has further shown that in these abnormal times, the Crisis Staff was the preeminent body, had authority over the executive committee. Mr. Kovacevic, who I believe is the signatory of this document, was on the Crisis Staff and it's our position he's under the influence and authority of Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think in this case, the parties can rely on the Judges' ability to read and to evaluate the documents later. I understand your objections in a system where we are working with a jury, which is not the case here. The documents are admitted into evidence ads S243A and B respectively. As regards the cross-examination, indeed, we have tomorrow, and on Thursday, I just learned that it is anticipated that it might take the entire time. We have the hearing in the morning and in the afternoon, but under these exceptional circumstances, first it might be possible, and we have to contact the responsible persons in this premises beforehand, to proceed a little bit longer, if necessary. And second, what I learned until now from Ms. Dahuron is that, in fact, the videoconference will bring us from 10.00 to 12.15. So therefore, the remaining time would be available. So I think if we all concentrate on the core issues, then it can be possible that we finalise the cross-examination by the end of Thursday afternoon. I can't see any objections. And I think it would be not fair to expect the Defence to start the cross-examination after this difficult day already now. Therefore, the trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 6.21 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 31st day of July, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
